passage:
Monday: Raghav came back from his night shift at the call centre to find the sink full: Hemant's dal pot, three mugs, a frying pan with egg stuck to it. He washed his own plate around them and said nothing.
Wednesday: Same pile, taller. Raghav had also covered the electricity bill again, and Hemant still hadn't transferred his half.
Thursday: The pot was growing something. Hemant was on the sofa, headphones on, laughing at a video. Raghav stood at the sink and said, loud enough, "Wow. Maybe the dishes will wash themselves if we believe hard enough." His voice had an edge he didn't recognise. It wasn't really the pot. It was feeling like the only adult in the flat, like nobody saw what he did.

qa.q: What had Raghav covered again by Wednesday?
qa.a: He had covered the electricity bill again.

qa.q: What is Raghav really feeling behind the sarcastic remark?
qa.a: He feels unseen and resentful, like the only adult in the flat, covering the bill and the dishes while nobody notices what he does.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Raghav at this first spark?
qa.a: He could name the real issue calmly, such as "I'm feeling taken for granted with the dishes and the bill, can we set up a system?", instead of sarcasm.

qa.q: How might Hemant hear the remark from the sofa?
qa.a: Hemant may hear only mockery out of nowhere, not knowing about the bill or the build-up, and feel attacked rather than asked.

grounding: Shows a flatmate whose sarcastic line about days-old dishes really comes from a quietly growing sense of being disrespected.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage: Your grandfather Gurpreet was not always this patient, Madhuri. At twenty-one I shared two rooms in Ludhiana with a boy called Satnam, both of us new at the textile mill. Every evening I came home to his tea glasses on the floor and his socks on my chair. Third day in a row, I picked up a glass and said, very sweetly, "Thank you, Satnam ji, for decorating our home." He laughed. I didn't. Later, lying awake, I understood it had nothing to do with glasses. I had been cooking for both of us for a month, and he had never once said it was good. I felt like a servant, not a friend. That is what the remark was really about. So when you complain about your flatmate's dishes, ask yourself what you are actually hungry for.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet share rooms at twenty-one?
qa.a: He shared two rooms in Ludhiana with Satnam, both new at the textile mill.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet realise he was really feeling that night?
qa.a: He realised he felt like a servant, not a friend, because he had cooked for a month without one word of thanks.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet advise Madhuri to do before complaining about a flatmate?
qa.a: To ask what one is actually hungry for, meaning the need underneath the complaint, before speaking.

qa.q: Why might Satnam have laughed at the remark?
qa.a: Satnam probably heard only a joke about glasses and had no idea about the month of unthanked cooking building up underneath.

grounding: Shows a young man's sarcastic remark about mess that is really about feeling unappreciated, told by him as an elder.

passage:
Tanvir and Bhaskar rented one room above the sweet shop in Barabanki while they trained at the block office. The water came only in the morning, so the rule was simple: wash your plate before the tap dried.
On Thursday evening Tanvir climbed the stairs and saw three days of plates in the bucket, flies circling the dal.
"Wah, Bhaskar-ji," he muttered, loud enough, "the king has left the palace dishes for his servant again."
Bhaskar looked up from his phone, surprised.
Tanvir didn't explain. It wasn't really the plates. It was that Bhaskar never asked before using his bucket, took the fan side of the room, and laughed when Tanvir called home to his mother.

qa.q: Why did the flatmates have to wash plates in the morning?
qa.a: Because the water came only in the morning.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he muttered about the king and his servant?
qa.a: He felt resentful and disrespected, a hurt that had been building over the bucket, the fan side and Bhaskar laughing at his calls home.

qa.q: What turning point is available before this becomes a real fight?
qa.a: Tanvir could calmly tell Bhaskar the bigger things that bother him, like the bucket and the laughing, instead of sarcasm about the plates.

qa.q: How might Bhaskar see the remark?
qa.a: He seems surprised and may feel attacked over a few dishes, not knowing about the other things Tanvir has been holding in.

grounding: A young man in a small-town shared room mutters sarcasm about piled dishes, though the real issue is a slow build-up of feeling disrespected.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage:
In the student flat in Amsterdam, Noa opened the kitchen door and stopped. The sink was full again, pans crusted from Esther's pasta on Sunday, and it was Wednesday.
"Oh great," Noa said to the empty room, then louder when Esther came in, "I love living in a restaurant where I'm the only one who washes up."
Esther paused with her keys still in her hand. "I was going to do it tonight."
"Sure you were."
Noa's cheeks were hot. It wasn't really the pans. It was that Esther's friends stayed over without asking, and Noa's notes on the fridge were ignored. It had been piling up quietly, like the dishes.

qa.q: Whose pasta pans were in the sink?
qa.a: Esther's, from Sunday.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling as she made the sarcastic remark?
qa.a: Noa felt resentful and disrespected; the pans stood for friends staying over without asking and fridge notes being ignored.

qa.q: What could Noa do at this stage to keep it from escalating?
qa.a: She could take a breath and say calmly what really bothers her, the overnight guests and ignored notes, instead of using sarcasm.

qa.q: How might Esther see the moment when she walks in?
qa.a: She seems caught off guard and may feel judged, since she planned to wash up tonight and doesn't see the bigger hurt.

grounding: A student makes a sarcastic remark about her flatmate's dishes, but underneath is a quietly growing sense of not being respected.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage:
The graduate residence at the university had four students to a kitchen, and on the third morning Madhuri opened the door to the same tower of plates in the sink.

Curry pan. Two mugs with tea rings. A plate with dried ketchup that she was fairly sure was Irfan's, since he'd made fries on Sunday.

Irfan wandered in, yawning.

"Oh good, the dishwasher's arrived," Madhuri said, not quite under her breath. "Do they teach washing up in your PhD, or is that beneath you?"

He blinked. "Morning to you too."

She slammed a cupboard harder than she meant to. It wasn't really the ketchup. It was the way her labelled milk kept vanishing, the way her notes on the fridge got moved, the way nobody seemed to notice she was the only one who ever cleaned. It had been building for weeks.

qa.q: How many students shared the kitchen?
qa.a: Four students shared a kitchen.

qa.q: What was Madhuri really upset about underneath the sarcasm?
qa.a: She felt unrespected and unseen, since her milk vanished, her notes were moved and nobody noticed that she did all the cleaning.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say instead of the sarcastic remark?
qa.a: She could tell Irfan and the others calmly that she feels she does most of the cleaning and ask to agree a plan together.

qa.q: How might Irfan see the moment?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt ambushed by a sharp comment first thing in the morning, without knowing the weeks of frustration behind it.

grounding: In a shared residence, a flatmate mutters sarcasm over dishes piled for days, while the real issue is a slowly building sense of disrespect.
